blocks.md: Factor-augmenting technology makes one particular input more productive, as if you had more of it. Better software can make each skilled worker do the work of two; better machines can make each unskilled worker more productive. Whether a gain for one input raises or lowers its pay depends on how easily the inputs substitute for each other — a surprising result. Growth models use the version that boosts labor, because it lets the economy grow at a steady pace.

blocks.title: Why it matters
blocks.md: It is the formal meaning of skill-biased technical change and of technological progress in growth models.

In the [CES Production Function](note:ces-production-function), $A_H$ and $A_L$ multiply the labour inputs: $A_H H$ is skilled labour measured in **efficiency units**. A rise in $A_H$ makes each skilled worker do the work of more skilled workers.

sections.heading: Does skill-augmenting technology raise the skill premium?

blocks.md:
- **$\sigma > 1$**: yes. Skilled workers become more productive and firms substitute toward them. This is **skill-biased technical change**.
- **$\sigma < 1$**: **no** — the premium *falls*. With complements, more productive skilled workers mean you need fewer of them to pair with unskilled labour.
- **$\sigma = 1$**: no effect (Cobb-Douglas).
That counter-intuitive $\sigma < 1$ case is a classic exam question. "Skill-augmenting" and "skill-biased" are the same thing **only** when $\sigma > 1$.

We can construct $w_{Ht}/w_{Lt}$ and $H_t/L_t$ from data, but **not** $A_{Ht}/A_{Lt}$. The [Canonical Model of the Skill Premium](note:canonical-model-of-the-skill-premium) handles this by assuming relative technology follows a time trend plus noise.

| Type | Production function | Augments |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hicks-neutral | $A\,F(K, L)$ | All inputs equally (TFP) |
| Harrod-neutral (labor-augmenting) | $F(K, AL)$ | Labor |
| Solow-neutral (capital-augmenting) | $F(AK, L)$ | Capital |

With a [Cobb-Douglas Production Function](note:cobb-douglas-production-function) the three are interchangeable: $AK^{\alpha}L^{1-\alpha} = K^{\alpha}(A^{1/(1-\alpha)}L)^{1-\alpha}$, so TFP growing at $\gamma$ is labor-augmenting growth at $\gamma/(1-\alpha)$. Outside Cobb-Douglas they differ — exactly the point of the $\sigma > 1$ condition above.
Growth models write technology as labor-augmenting so that dividing by effective labor $\tilde{A}L$ removes all trend growth ([Balanced Growth Path](note:balanced-growth-path)).

blocks.title: Beyond the notes
blocks.md: Uzawa's theorem: for a balanced growth path to exist with a general production function, technical change must be labor-augmenting.
